report:
**Conclusion: The evidence supports "no" — saw palmetto does not provide meaningful long-term symptom improvement over placebo for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH).**

The strongest evidence comes from a **Cochrane systematic review** (MacDonald et al.), which pooled multiple randomized controlled trials of Serenoa repens (saw palmetto) monotherapy for BPH-related lower urinary tract symptoms. The review explicitly concluded that "these trials found Serenoa repens no better than placebo, even (in one trial) at escalating doses" — https://www.researchgate.net/publication/224887169_Serenoa_repens_monotherapy_for_benign_prostatic_hyperplasia_BPH_An_updated_Cochrane_systematic_review

This is corroborated by the **CAMUS trial** (Complementary and Alternative Medicine for Urological Symptoms), a large, well-designed, dose-escalation randomized trial that tested standard and triple doses of saw palmetto over 18 months. While its primary focus in the retrieved source was safety, the trial is widely cited (including by the NCCIH) as finding no symptom benefit over placebo even at higher doses — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3716255/

The **NCCIH (National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health)**, a U.S. government authority, summarizes the state of evidence clearly: "a large study evaluating high doses of saw palmetto and a Cochrane review found that saw palmetto was not more effective than placebo for treatment of urinary symptoms related to BPH" — https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/providers/digest/spotlight-on-saw-palmetto-science

Together, these sources — a rigorous Cochrane meta-analysis, a large-scale dose-escalation RCT, and an authoritative government health summary — converge on the same conclusion: despite earlier smaller studies suggesting modest benefits, higher-quality and longer-term evidence shows saw palmetto does not outperform placebo for BPH symptoms.
